expedition_metadata.user_query: Why do cats knead with their paws before they lie down?

journey_deck.heading: Making Biscuits
body_markdown: Watch a cat before it settles down and you'll see it: paws pressing rhythmically into a blanket, a cushion, sometimes your leg. Left paw, right paw, left paw, over and over.
Cat owners call it 'making biscuits.' It looks playful, but it's actually one of the most consistent, hard-wired behaviors in the entire species.

journey_deck.heading: Where It Starts: The Nursing Reflex
body_markdown: Kittens knead their mother's belly while nursing. The pressing motion physically stimulates the mammary glands and helps trigger milk letdown - the release of milk into the ducts so the kitten can feed.

It works because the kitten's brain pairs the motion with a flood of comfort: **the kneading reflex gets wired directly to feeling safe and fed**, weeks before the kitten has any other way to understand the world.

journey_deck.heading: So why do grown cats - who aren't nursing, and have no mother's belly in sight - still do it?

options.label: It's a leftover reflex from kittenhood that never switched off
It's a sign the cat is in physical pain
It's an attempt to dig a hole

reveal_payload.feedback_text: Right - it's a **retained reflex**. The muscle memory and the emotional payoff (comfort, safety) stay linked long after the original reason - milk - disappears. That's why kneading shows up almost exclusively when a cat already feels relaxed.

journey_deck.heading: A Second Reason: Scent
body_markdown: Cats have scent glands in their paw pads. Every knead presses a small amount of that scent - a chemical signal called a **pheromone** - into whatever surface they're pushing on.
That's a second, independent reason kneading persists: it's a quiet way of marking a spot as theirs, safe, and already claimed - right before they commit to lying down on it.

journey_deck.heading: A Third Reason: An Old Habit From the Wild
body_markdown: Domestic cats' wild ancestors didn't have cushions. Before lying down in tall grass or leaves, a wild cat would press and pat the ground flat, testing it and softening it into a nest.
Many researchers think that pressing motion is the same one you see today - just aimed at a blanket instead of a patch of grass.

journey_deck.heading: Quick check: which of these is the strongest sign that kneading is a comfort behavior rather than random fidgeting?

options.label: Cats knead almost exclusively when they're relaxed, right before settling down or being petted
Cats knead the fastest right after a meal

journey_deck.correct_feedback: Exactly. Kneading clusters around moments of relaxation and pre-sleep settling - not eating, not play, not stress. That timing is the biggest clue it's tied to comfort, not appetite or excitement.
journey_deck.incorrect_feedback: Not quite - kneading doesn't actually spike right after meals. The real tell is timing: it shows up almost entirely in relaxed, pre-sleep, being-petted moments, which is why comfort, not food, is the throughline.

payoff_layer.explain_it_back_prompt: In one sentence: why does an adult cat, far from any mother's belly, still knead before lying down?

mint_card.title: The Kitten Reflex That Never Left
mint_card.shareable_synthesis: A cat kneading a blanket is running a nursing reflex from kittenhood - now repurposed for comfort, scent-marking, and nest-making all at once.
